blocks.text: Introduction

Analytical geometry (also called coordinate geometry) is the branch of mathematics that joins algebra and geometry. Instead of only drawing or imagining shapes, lines and figures, we describe them with points and equations on the xy-plane. This makes it easy to calculate distances, mid-points, slopes and points of intersection, and to solve practical problems such as finding the shortest path, checking whether two lines are parallel, or locating the exact position of an object.

Analytical geometry was developed in the 17th century by the French mathematician René Descartes, who introduced the idea of using coordinates to represent geometric figures. His work became the link between algebra and geometry and laid the foundation of modern mathematics.

In this unit we study straight lines, angles between coplanar intersecting lines, the concurrency of medians, right bisectors and altitudes of a triangle, the area of a triangular region, and applications of analytical geometry to real-life problems.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Three tools from Class XI are used on every page of this unit. Revise them now:
1. Slope of the line through \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \((x_{2}, y_{2})\):
\[m = \dfrac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}\]
It tells how much \(y\) rises when \(x\) increases by 1. If the line makes angle \(\alpha\) with the positive x-axis, \(m = \tan\alpha\).
2. Mid-point of the segment joining \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \((x_{2}, y_{2})\):
\[\left(\dfrac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2}, \dfrac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}\right)\]
3. A point lies on a line exactly when its coordinates satisfy the line's equation. This is how we check every answer.
We have learnt that in coordinate geometry, a straight line can be represented in different forms depending on the information given.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: A straight line is fixed completely by two pieces of information: a point and a direction (slope), or two points, or the two intercepts, or its distance from the origin and the direction of the perpendicular. Each piece of information leads to its own form of the equation. All the forms below describe the same kind of object; after simplifying, every one of them becomes \(ax + by + c = 0\).
General Form
The general form of a straight line in two variables is written as \(ax + by + c = 0\), where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are real numbers and \(a\) and \(b\) are not simultaneously zero.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why must \(a\) and \(b\) not both be zero? If \(a = b = 0\), the equation becomes \(c = 0\): there is no \(x\) and no \(y\) left, so it describes no line at all. Also, multiplying the whole equation by any non-zero number gives the same line: \(2x - y - 6 = 0\) and \(4x - 2y - 12 = 0\) are one and the same line. We usually remove common factors and fractions, and make the coefficient of \(x\) positive.
Slope-Intercept Form
If \(m\) is the slope and \(c\) is the y-intercept of a line, then equation of this straight line in slope-intercept form is \(y = mx + c\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Here the y-intercept \(c\) means the line cuts the y-axis at the point \((0, c)\). Put \(x = 0\) in \(y = mx + c\) and you get \(y = c\). Use this form when the slope and the y-intercept are given, or when you want to read the slope off an equation: solve for \(y\), and the number in front of \(x\) is the slope.
Point-Slope Form
If a line passes through a point \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) and has slope \(m\), then equation of straight line in point slope form is \(y - y_{1} = m(x - x_{1})\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where does it come from? Take any other point \((x, y)\) on the line. The slope between \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \((x, y)\) must be \(m\):
\[\dfrac{y - y_{1}}{x - x_{1}} = m\]
Multiply by \(x - x_{1}\) and you have the point-slope form. This is the most used form in this unit: medians, altitudes and right bisectors are all written with it.
Two-Point Form

If a line passes through two points \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \((x_{2}, y_{2})\), then equation of straight line in two-point form is
\[\dfrac{y - y_{2}}{y_{2} - y_{1}} = \dfrac{x - x_{2}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}\]
or
\[\dfrac{y - y_{1}}{y_{1} - y_{2}} = \dfrac{x - x_{1}}{x_{1} - x_{2}}\]
or
\[y - y_{1} = \dfrac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}(x - x_{1})\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The third version shows the idea clearly: first find the slope \(m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}\) from the two points, then use the point-slope form. The first two versions are the same equation written with fractions. If \(x_{1} = x_{2}\), the slope is undefined and the line is simply \(x = x_{1}\) (a vertical line).
Intercept Form

If \(a\) and \(b\) are the x-intercept and y-intercept of the line, then equation of straight line in intercept form is
\[\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Check: put \(y = 0\), you get \(x = a\), so the line meets the x-axis at \((a, 0)\); put \(x = 0\), you get \(y = b\), so it meets the y-axis at \((0, b)\). The intercepts may be negative. This form cannot be used for a line through the origin (both intercepts are 0) or for a line parallel to an axis.
Normal Form

\(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = p\) is an equation of the straight line, where \(p\) is the perpendicular distance of the line from the origin and \(\theta\) is the angle made by perpendicular with the positive x-axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Picture it: draw the perpendicular from the origin \(O\) to the line. Its length is \(p\) (so \(p \ge 0\)) and it makes angle \(\theta\) with the positive x-axis. Its foot is the point
\[N(p\cos\theta, p\sin\theta)\]
The line passes through \(N\) and is perpendicular to \(ON\). The word 'normal' means perpendicular. In this form the right-hand side \(p\) is never negative, and the coefficients satisfy \(\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta = 1\).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.problem: Find an equation of the straight line if its slope is 3 and y-intercept is 7.
steps:
Given: slope \(m = 3\), y-intercept \(c = 7\).
To find: the equation of the line.
Method: slope and y-intercept are given, so the slope-intercept form \(y = mx + c\) fits directly.

Write the given values
The slope and y-intercept of the line are respectively:
\[m = 3, \quad c = 7\]
Why: we must identify \(m\) and \(c\) before substituting.

Substitute in the slope-intercept form
Thus, slope-intercept form of a line is:
\[y = mx + c\]
\[y = 3x + 7\]
Why: the form needs exactly these two numbers, nothing else.

Check:
At \(x = 0\): \(y = 7\), so the line cuts the y-axis at \((0, 7)\). From \(x = 0\) to \(x = 1\), \(y\) goes from 7 to 10, a rise of 3, so the slope is 3.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.problem: Write down an equation of the straight line passing through \((-4, 3)\) and having slope \(-5\).
steps:
Given: point \((x_{1}, y_{1}) = (-4, 3)\), slope \(m = -5\).
To find: the equation of the line.
Method: one point and the slope are given, so the point-slope form \(y - y_{1} = m(x - x_{1})\) fits.

Substitute in the point-slope form
As the point \((-4, 3)\) lies on the required line having slope \(-5\), so by point-slope form of equation of the straight line, we have
\[y - 3 = -5(x - (-4))\]
\[y - 3 = -5(x + 4)\]
Why: \(x_{1} = -4\), so \(x - x_{1} = x - (-4) = x + 4\). Keep the brackets; the minus signs are where most errors happen.

Expand and simplify
\[y - 3 = -5x - 20\]
\[5x + y + 17 = 0\]
which is an equation of the required line.
Why: we add \(5x + 20\) to both sides to bring every term to the left, giving the general form.

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.problem: Find an equation of the straight line passing through the points \((-3, -2)\) and \((5, 4)\).
steps:
Given: \((x_{1}, y_{1}) = (-3, -2)\) and \((x_{2}, y_{2}) = (5, 4)\).
To find: the equation of the line through them.
Method: two points are given, so the two-point form fits.

Write the two-point form
Using two-point form of an equation of the straight line, the required equation is
\[\dfrac{y - (-2)}{4 - (-2)} = \dfrac{x - (-3)}{5 - (-3)}\]
\[\dfrac{y + 2}{6} = \dfrac{x + 3}{8}\]
Why: \(\frac{y - y_{1}}{y_{2} - y_{1}} = \frac{x - x_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}\); subtracting a negative number means adding.

Clear the fractions
\[y + 2 = \dfrac{6}{8}(x + 3)\]
\[8(y + 2) = 6(x + 3)\]
Why: cross-multiplication removes both denominators.

Simplify to general form
\[8y + 16 = 6x + 18\]
\[6x - 8y + 2 = 0\]
\[3x - 4y + 1 = 0\]
Why: move everything to one side, then divide by the common factor 2.

blocks.title: Example 4
blocks.problem: Write down an equation of the straight line which cuts the x-axis at \((3, 0)\) and y-axis at \((0, -6)\).
steps:
Given: the line meets the x-axis at \((3, 0)\) and the y-axis at \((0, -6)\).
To find: the equation of the line.
Method: both intercepts are known: \(a = 3\), \(b = -6\). Use the two-intercept form \(\frac{x}{a} + \frac{y}{b} = 1\).

Substitute the intercepts
As 3 and \(-6\) are x and y-intercepts respectively of the required line, so by two-intercepts form of an equation of the straight line, we have
\[\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{-6} = 1\]
Why: an intercept is the coordinate where the line crosses the axis, with its sign; the y-intercept is \(-6\), not 6.

Clear the fractions
\[2x - y = 6\]
\[2x - y - 6 = 0\]
which is the required equation.
Why: multiply both sides by 6, the L.C.M. of 3 and 6: \(6 \cdot \frac{x}{3} = 2x\) and \(6 \cdot \frac{y}{-6} = -y\).

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem: The length of perpendicular from the origin to a line is 3 units and the inclination of this perpendicular is \(120^\circ\). Find the equation of the straight line.
steps:
Given: \(p = 3\), \(\theta = 120^\circ\).
To find: the equation of the line.
Method: the distance of the line from the origin and the angle of the perpendicular are given; that is exactly the information of the normal form \(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = p\).

Write the normal form
Equation of the straight line in normal form is:
\[x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = p\]
\[x\cos 120^\circ + y\sin 120^\circ = 3\]
Why: we only substitute \(\theta\) and \(p\).

Put the trigonometric values
\[-\dfrac{1}{2}x + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}y = 3\]
Why: \(120^\circ\) is in the second quadrant: \(\cos 120^\circ = -\cos 60^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\sin 120^\circ = \sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

Simplify
\[x - \sqrt{3}y = -6\]
\[x - \sqrt{3}y + 6 = 0\]
Why: multiply both sides by \(-2\) to clear the fractions and make the coefficient of \(x\) positive (every term changes sign).

Check:
Distance from the origin \(= \frac{|6|}{\sqrt{1 + 3}} = \frac{6}{2} = 3 = p\). The foot of the perpendicular \((3\cos 120^\circ, 3\sin 120^\circ) = (-\frac{3}{2}, \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2})\) satisfies the equation: \(-\frac{3}{2} - \frac{9}{2} + 6 = 0\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. General form: \(ax + by + c = 0\), \(a\) and \(b\) not both zero. Every form simplifies to it.
2. Slope-intercept \(y = mx + c\); point-slope \(y - y_{1} = m(x - x_{1})\); two-point: find \(m\) from the points, then point-slope.
3. Intercept form \(\frac{x}{a} + \frac{y}{b} = 1\): \(a\), \(b\) are the signed intercepts.
4. Normal form \(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = p\): \(p \ge 0\) is the distance from the origin, \(\theta\) the angle of the perpendicular.
5. Always check: the given point(s) must satisfy your final equation.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Sign errors with negative coordinates: \(x - (-4) = x + 4\), not \(x - 4\).
2. Writing the y-intercept as a point: the y-intercept is the number \(c\); the point is \((0, c)\).
3. In intercept form, dropping the minus sign of a negative intercept: \(\frac{y}{-6}\), not \(\frac{y}{6}\).
4. In normal form, using the angle of the line instead of the angle of the perpendicular, or taking \(\cos 120^\circ = +\frac{1}{2}\).
5. Forgetting to multiply every term when clearing fractions.
